core_message: The Antikythera mechanism, found in a shipwreck in 1901, is a 2,000-year-old Greek gear computer that predicted eclipses.
title: A Computer Found in an Ancient Shipwreck
description:
In 1900, Greek sponge divers sheltering from a storm near the island of Antikythera found a Roman-era shipwreck full of statues and treasure. In 1901 they brought up corroded lumps of bronze that turned out to be the Antikythera mechanism, a hand-cranked device made in Greece in roughly the 2nd or 1st century BC. Housed in a wooden case, it used at least 30 interlocking bronze gears to show the positions of the Sun and Moon, the Moon's phases, eclipse predictions years ahead, and the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games including the Olympics. It is often called the oldest known analogue computer; nothing of comparable complexity is known until medieval astronomical clocks more than a thousand years later. The fragments are in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. The gear layout shown here is illustrative, not an exact reconstruction.

Source: Wikipedia, Antikythera mechanism.

scenes.narration: Divers pulled this lump of corroded bronze out of a shipwreck in 1901. Inside it is a computer more than two thousand years old.
Greek sponge divers sheltering from a storm near the island of Antikythera found a Roman-era wreck full of treasure, and among it, a few pieces of bronze.
It was a hand-cranked machine in a wooden box. Turn the handle, and pointers showed where the Sun and Moon would be, and even the Moon's phases.
Inside were at least thirty interlocking bronze gears. It could predict eclipses years ahead, and even kept track of the Olympic Games.
Nothing this complex is known again for more than a thousand years. Today its pieces sit in a museum in Athens.
